Agnes Wickfield. A principal character in Charles Dickens's novel David Copperfield, serving as David's loyal friend and conscience and eventual wife. Defined by selflessness and moral constancy and quiet intelligence, Agnes represents the ideal Victorian woman: dutiful and nurturing and morally steadfast. Her relationship with David anchors the novel's exploration of maturation and the meaning of home.

She is the daughter of a lawyer named Wickfield, whom she supports by managing the household while he falls under the influence of the scheming Uriah Heep. Characterized by her composure and kindness and almost ethereal virtue, Dickens portrays her as nearly too good to be real. She harbors deep affection for David from their first meeting, which David initially fails to recognize or reciprocate. As the novel progresses, Agnes serves as David's confidante and advisor, offering steady moral guidance as he navigates the misadventures and disappointments of his youth.

A victim of Uriah Heep's schemes, she endures his unwanted courtship and manipulation as part of his larger plot to control her father and his business. Her constancy stands in sharp contrast to David's youthful confusion and the duplicity of other characters. She represents a strain of idealized womanhood in Victorian literature: the patient, self-sacrificing partner who waits and supports rather than pursuing her own ambitions. Her ultimate union with David symbolizes his spiritual and emotional maturation, and her steadiness becomes the foundation of his adult happiness.

Literary critics have debated whether Agnes represents genuine characterization or an idealized archetype too perfect to be psychologically credible. Her passivity contrasts with modern expectations of female agency. Her character embodies and tests themes of virtue and morality in literature. She shares the novel with David Copperfield, whose relationship with her is central to the plot, with Uriah Heep, who serves as her antagonist, with Charles Dickens, her creator who exemplifies his idealized portrayal of virtuous femininity.
